1:
Whose voice it is that gives the order is settled by an argument from the previous chapter. Robertson points out that it cannot be an angel, as elsewhere in the book, because the temple had been filled with smoke so that no one could enter it; the voice must therefore be God's own. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by looking forward instead of back: the voice that later announces that it is done is expressly said to come from the throne, and this first voice is most likely the same. Gill leaves the question open and canvasses three answers. It may be the voice of God, whose temple the church is and who roars out of Zion when he brings judgment on the earth; or of Christ, who is always in the midst of his people and whose voice is as the voice of many waters; or of one of the four living creatures through whom Christ often speaks — an option Gill rather favours, since it was one of those who had handed the seven angels the golden vials they are now told to pour out. Ellicott notes that the vials are poured, in the Greek, into the earth rather than merely upon it.

Henry fastens on the delay and what ends it. Everything had been made ready in the previous vision, yet nothing was to be executed without an immediate positive order from God — and that order comes out of the temple, which he reads as God answering the prayers of his people and avenging their quarrel. Clarke states the same principle as a rule: these ministers of divine justice stood ready and had full power, but could do nothing until they received an express commission, since nothing whatever is done without the permission of God. Henry then turns to the obedience. No sooner was the command given than it was obeyed, with no delay and no objection raised; and he cannot help contrasting the angels with better-known servants, since some of the best men, Moses and Jeremiah among them, did not so readily come in and comply with the call of God to their work. The angels excel not only in strength but in readiness to do his will, which is why we are taught to pray that his will may be done on earth as it is done in heaven.

On the shape of the series Wesley offers the neatest observation in the chapter. The letters to the seven churches divide three and four; the seals, trumpets and vials divide the other way, four and three. The trumpets overthrow the kingdom of the world gradually and over a long tract of time, while the vials destroy chiefly the beast and his followers with a swift and impetuous force; and of the seven, the first four fall on earth, sea, rivers and sun, while the last three fall elsewhere and are much more terrible. Henry adds two structural points. The vials allude throughout to the plagues of Egypt, the waters turned to blood and the smiting with boils, because the sins were alike and so were the punishments; and they answer to the seven trumpets which had described the rise of antichrist, so that his fall bears a resemblance to his rise and God brings men down by the very means they chose to exalt themselves. Barnes reads the whole as the successive blows by which the Papacy will fall, and is candid that part of it remains future — admitting more difficulty in satisfying the mind here than in the portions that pertain to past events.
2:
Both plagues are read against Egypt. Clarke identifies the first as the sixth Egyptian plague of boils and blains, and Robertson supplies the word — an old term for a suppurated wound — noting that where the magicians were the ones attacked in Egypt, here it is the worshippers of the beast. On the second he observes that only the Nile was affected in the older plague, while here it is the sea entire, and that the phrase about a dead man is added to the Egyptian text: the picture, in Swete's phrase, of a murdered man weltering in his blood, or in Moffatt's, of coagulated blood fatal to animal life. He notes too that the destruction is complete rather than partial as at the corresponding trumpet, where only a third died. Ellicott draws out the aptness of the Egyptian parallel: the plagues there struck at the very things Egypt drew its strength from, so that the Nile became worse than useless when turned to blood — and here the sea, out of which the beast rose and from which the world-power drew its strength, is the thing corrupted. Wesley adds that the Hebrews supposed the Egyptian plagues a month apart, and wonders whether the vials may be spaced likewise.

Whether any of this is to be taken literally is the chapter's dividing question, and these two verses bring it to a head at once. Wesley is the plainest: the vial was poured on the earth, literally taken; the ulcer fell on those who had the mark, all of them and them only; and all these plagues seem to him to be described in proper and not figurative words — with the consequence, which he states without hedging, that they are all yet to come. Ellicott takes the opposite view as settled. Egypt is one type of the world-power and the plagues are used as types too, not to be understood literally; the evil sore accordingly denotes some throbbing and hateful affliction, perhaps mental or spiritual, which breaks in on the serenity and self-complacency of those who worship the world-power. He extends the same reading to the sea, which stands for the tumultuous impulses of the masses — a healthy force when ruled by God, melodious as the voice of the ocean, but corrupt and deadly when swayed by mere impulse or directed by worldliness, so that it kills every token of better life. Gill agrees that the sea is not literal, but for quite different reasons.

Gill's reason is historical rather than moral. The sea is a collection of many waters, and many waters in this book mean the peoples under the Roman yoke, so he takes it for the whole jurisdiction of mystical Babylon and particularly its maritime powers, Spain and Portugal — the more readily because the second trumpet, which also struck the sea, had brought the Vandals into those same countries. He reports the identifications others have made and rejects one flatly: the first angel cannot be Pope Adrian, as a Roman interpreter proposed, since a pope would never hurt the worshippers of the beast; Brightman's application of it to Queen Elizabeth he passes on without endorsing, preferring some set of princes still to come. Barnes reads the whole chapter as the successive blows by which the Papacy falls, and takes the blood as of a dead man to suggest naval conflict, the discoloured water indicating blood shed in quantity on the waters. Clarke reaches the same conclusion in two sentences, calling it the most probable meaning of the vial: engagements so sanguinary that conquerors and conquered were nearly destroyed together, and the sea tinged with the blood of the slain.
4:
The third vial completes the ruin of the water. Robertson notes only that contamination of the fresh supply follows that of the sea and is again total; Clarke traces it to the first Egyptian plague and reports the rabbinic maxim behind the whole chapter — that whatever plagues God inflicted on the Egyptians of old he will inflict on the enemies of his people in all later times. Ellicott presses the symbolism further than anyone. The streams and springs feed the sea, and stand for the powers and influences that go to make up popular sentiment, so that the same corruption which spoils the sea works back up every tributary. Men cannot worship worldliness, he argues, without degrading those who supply their instruction and their recreations to the same level; when public taste grows corrupt the literature follows, the up-flowing tide colouring the down-coming stream, since the morality of a nation's art always rises no higher than the morality of its manners. Wesley says simply that the waters were over all the earth and that none could drink of them.

Gill and Barnes both look for the fulfilment in Europe. Gill rules out a literal drying up and proposes instead the writings of the most learned and subtle men of Rome, who like springs feed and sustain that jurisdiction, together with their confutation by Protestant writers and the destruction of the principal orders — cardinals, bishops, Jesuits. But he thinks the geography chiefly meant is Italy and Savoy, on the ground that the third trumpet, which also struck rivers and fountains, brought the Huns into Italy; the third vial will bring wars and bloodshed to the very places where so much of the blood of the saints was shed. Barnes reasons from the same parallel with more restraint, saying only that the analogy would lead us to look for similar desolations in those parts of Europe, and that the waters becoming blood would be fulfilled if bloody battles were fought near them so that they seemed to run red.

"The angel of the waters" sends them all to the rabbis. Clarke reports that angels were assigned not merely to the four elements but to almost everything — an angel of the earth named Admael, one over the grass, another over the cattle that feed on it, and an angel of the sea named Rahab whom God employed to swallow the waters at creation and slew for disobeying — and judges that the writer of the Apocalypse plainly keeps these notions in view. Robertson and Barnes note the same background more soberly. Gill adds a suggestion from Lightfoot that is entirely his own: since these angels appear in the dress of priests, and since a priest was appointed to look after the wells and ditches round Jerusalem so that the people might have water at the feasts, there may be an allusion to that office — one Nechoniah held it, and after him a Nicodemon ben Gorion whom some identify with the Nicodemus of the Gospels. Wesley notices which title God is given at this point, and why: at the opening of the book he is called the Almighty, when his patience is being praised; now that vengeance is abroad, he is called the Gracious One.
6:
The sentence is retribution measured out, and the commentators press the exactness of it. Robertson makes the noun for blood the emphatic word, measure for measure against those who shed the blood of saints and prophets, and notes that the perfect tense makes the punishment permanent as well as just; there was no drinking water left, only this coagulated blood. Wesley observes the aptness of the figure, that men do not drink out of the sea but out of springs and rivers, so the sentence is fitly attached to this vial and not the last. Ellicott corrects the tenses and removes the connecting word: not because they have shed, but because they shed, and blood didst thou give them — a sentence, he says, with a startling force which the conjunction only weakens. Barnes takes the prophets in the ordinary New Testament sense of teachers of religion rather than inspired men, so that the blood avenged is that of private believers and public teachers together. Gill turns the argument round to prove his reading of the previous verses: since it is blood-guilt that is punished here, the rivers and fountains cannot have been literal at all, but men.

Clarke alone supplies a parallel from outside Scripture, and it is the sharpest thing in the entry. When Tomyris, queen of the Scythians, had defeated Cyrus, she cut off his head and threw it into a vessel of blood with the words: satisfy thyself with the blood for which thou hast thirsted and of which thy desire has been insatiable. This figure of speech, Clarke notes, rhetoric calls sarcasm, and he quotes the old couplet on it — that sarcasm kills with this biting taunt, Cyrus, thy thirst was blood, now drink thy fill. Gill fills in the geography he had already argued for, observing how much of the blood of the saints and of the preachers of the gospel was shed in Italy and Savoy and the places near Rome, as well as in Rome itself. Barnes is careful about what the retribution does and does not imply, since those suffering now need not be the same individuals who shed the blood.

The answering voice at the altar raises a small textual question. Barnes takes it for another angel, either the one presiding over the altar or one whose voice seemed to come from it, and connects the scene with the martyrs seen earlier under the altar crying for their blood to be avenged — though he does not think the two visions the same. Gill reports that the Ethiopic version makes the speaker the angel of the fountains again, while the Alexandrian copy and the Syriac and Arabic read that he heard the altar itself speaking. Ellicott adopts precisely that reading, translating not another out of the altar but the altar saying — the altar beneath which the martyrs cried and on which the prayers of the saints were offered now confirming the testimony to the justice of God. Robertson observes that the address matches the Song of Moses two chapters earlier, with judgments put where ways had stood and the two adjectives reversed. Wesley notes that the voice answers the angel of the waters, affirming of God's judgments in general what had been said of one in particular.
8:
Robertson marks the difference from the corresponding trumpet: there a third of sun, moon and stars was struck with darkness, here the sun is struck with extreme heat, and the added phrase about fire intensifies the picture. Wesley notices the pattern the four make together, affecting earth, water, fire and air in turn, and observes the plain resemblance between the first three vials and the first three trumpets. Gill refuses a literal reading and offers an unexpected one: the sun is Christ, and what scorches is the clear shining of him in the ministry of the word, which will not savingly enlighten the antichristian party but will convict and confound them, filling them with rage precisely because they cannot obscure the light or stop its progress. Barnes keeps to the general sense, that it cannot be supposed the sun was literally made hotter, and that the calamity is one under which human life itself would be cut down.

Two of them name the fulfilment, and one of the two records a prediction. Henry takes the sun for some eminent prince of the Roman communion who renounces that religion shortly before its downfall — some, he reports, expect it to be the German emperor — so that the very sun which had cherished the idolaters with benign influence now grows hot against them, princes using their power to suppress them. Clarke supplies something rarer: Robert Fleming, writing more than a century before him, had taken the sun for the French empire and conjectured that this vial would be poured out on it about the year 1794. Clarke sets the date beside the event and calls it remarkable, since in 1793 the French king was beheaded by the National Assembly, and unparalleled miseries followed which nearly extinguished the nobility and brought on a war of twenty-three years that came near to ruining France and the nations of Europe with her.

That the plague produces no repentance is what the commentators dwell on. Robertson calls the negative a refrain running like a funeral dirge through these chapters, and draws the conclusion the text forces: even deserved punishment may harden the heart. Barnes reads it as predicting a state of things in which wickedness and irreligion actually increase under judgment, men growing worse rather than better for what has come upon them. Wesley states the paradox exactly — they could not but acknowledge the hand of God, and yet hardened themselves against him. Clarke applies it to the events he had just described, and writes as a man reporting rather than expounding: no moral or national amendment followed those calamities in that unhappy country, nor in any of the nations engaged against her in the long and ruinous contest, which had now ended, he notes in 1817, without producing one political, moral or religious advantage either to France or to Europe. Gill sees in the scorching heat the rage and envy of men watching the antichristian state lose its head.
10:
Ellicott reads the sequence of vials as a moral pathology rather than a series of blows. The judgments gradually dissolve the integrity and organisation of the beast's kingdom by letting the principles it was built on work themselves out: first moral disease in individuals, then a corrupt tone of national morals spreading upward into the higher orders, then the fierce pride of vaunted light that scorches. Where those three are present, he says, disorganisation is not far off — evil goes out a murderer and comes home a suicide. The darkening he takes as the counterpart of the Egyptian plague, with a particular aptness: the kingdom that boasted itself so full of light becomes dark, since when men shut out the higher light the smoke of their own candles soon obscures the whole heaven. Robertson supplies the grammar and the vocabulary. The throne is Rome, given to the beast by the dragon; the darkening stands in a periphrastic pluperfect, so that the earlier plagues are still in force; and the verb for gnawing the tongue is an old word for chewing, found nowhere else in the New Testament.

On where the blow falls they largely agree. Gill identifies the throne with Rome, which was Satan's seat while the empire was pagan and was handed to the beast when he rose, and reports Daubuz's application of the plague to the expulsion of the western and eastern emperors from their capitals. Barnes narrows it further, to the Vatican itself, and is unusually explicit about what his reading commits him to: that the blow follows soon after the previous ones, that it falls on the central power of the Papacy and on the Pope personally, that it brings deep distress and darkness on those dominions, and that impiety will increase rather than diminish under it. Wesley reads the wording closely and draws an odd inference: it is not said upon the beast and his throne, so perhaps the beast will then be absent from it. He also sets out the geography of the series, the four first vials going round the whole earth as the four first trumpets did, and the three last running lengthways in a straight line — the fifth concerning the throne of the beast, the sixth the Mahometans, the seventh chiefly the heathens.

Clarke, who had lately been so confident about the French empire, turns sceptical here, and his aside is the most valuable sentence in the entry. Some, he reports, take the sun for the emperor Vitellius and the throne for Rome, the darkening being the loss of political consequence in the civil wars from which she never wholly recovered; others apply the whole to papal Rome, and on that reading, he says with visible dryness, make out a very clear case. Then the question: thus have men conjectured, but how much nearer are we to the truth? Robertson observes that the blaspheming and the impenitence are word for word what stood two verses earlier, with the sores now in the plural and the deeds added, and likens the pride to Nebuchadnezzar's against the God of heaven. Wesley notes the same doubling of the plural, taking it to mean that the pains and ulcers were greatly heightened and multiplied, and reads the gnawing of tongues as furious impatience. Gill adds only that the blasphemers curse the one who is of right their King.
12:
Ellicott gives the river its symbolic value first. In the long struggle between the kingdom of Christ and the world, the Euphrates stands for the great separating boundary between them, as the literal river formed the barrier between Israel and the hostile kingdoms to the north and east; it is the impediment that keeps war from breaking out. He identifies it with the restraint of public opinion, which holds evil back from its ruder and more violent forms, since men may be hostile to spiritual religion and still be unwilling to shock public sentiment — a barrier that can be dried up when false principles have been taught long enough and corrupt manners tolerated. Robertson keeps to the historical picture, of kings from the east marching against Rome, and notes that Parthia in particular had resisted Rome before Trajan's day. Barnes and Henry both look to the Turkish power, since the corresponding trumpet was referred to it, though Henry reports the rival view that the river meant is the Tiber, on the ground that if Rome is mystical Babylon then Tiber is mystical Euphrates, and that when Rome falls her river and her merchandise must suffer with her.

Wesley offers a chronological argument that none of the others attempt. Roman and Mahometan affairs, he holds, ran nearly parallel for several ages: in the seventh century came Mahomet, and a little before him Boniface with his universal bishopric; in the eleventh both the Turks and Gregory carried all before them; in the year 1300 Boniface appeared with his two swords at the newly erected jubilee, and in that self-same year — on the same day, he insists — arose the Ottoman Porte. It is on that parallel that he reads the vial poured on the beast's throne as followed immediately by the vial on the Euphrates. Gill takes the opposite tack and clears the ground by elimination: the drying is not literal, and it cannot be for the return of the Jews from the east, since no great number of them lives beyond that river, the far greater part being in the western and northern parts of the world. Clarke, characteristically, will not commit himself at all. He allows that an allusion to Cyrus's ruin of Babylon is likely, but adds that what city or people this Babylon means it is vain to conjecture.

The three frogs are read as emissaries, and the identifications differ widely. Robertson notes the structure — one evil spirit from the mouth of each of the three powers, the mouth being throughout this book the seat of influence — so that the sixth vial brings the dragon and his two subalterns back on stage together. Wesley distributes their hostility: the dragon fights chiefly against God, the beast against Christ, the false prophet against the Spirit of truth, and the three spirits that resemble them set about blackening the works of creation, redemption and sanctification. He adds a comparison that reverses the expected order, that Mahomet was first a false prophet and afterwards a powerful prince, whereas this beast was first powerful as a prince and afterwards became a teacher of lies. Barnes turns to Bochart for the force of the symbol, where the frog stands for a rough and coarse voice and so for querulous reproaching. Gill names cardinals, priests and particularly Jesuits, and reports Daubuz's threefold division into monks, religious knights and secular clergy; Clarke suggests false teachers generally, and mentions that some good critics have applied the passage to Vespasian and his pretended miracles.
14:
The signs the spirits work are not conceded to be miracles. Barnes takes them as wonders sufficient to deceive the world into believing them miraculous, and no more. Robertson supplies a lineage for them — the Egyptian magicians wrought signs, and so did Simon Magus and, later, Apollonius of Tyana — and reaches for a contemporary instance, noting Houdini's claim that he could reproduce every trick of the spiritualistic mediums. On the object of the mission, Barnes observes that no class of men has ever been more under the influence of pagan superstition, Mahometan delusion or the Papacy than kings and rulers, and expects that to continue. Robertson reads the gathering as a real world war and quotes Swete for the puzzle it presents: there have been times when nations were seized by a passion for war that the historian can only imperfectly explain. Gill keeps to the parentage of the spirits, that they are of their father the devil and do his lusts, being murderers and liars after his pattern.

The sudden first-person interruption is noticed by all of them. Gill takes the voice for Christ's own, breaking into the account to warn his people, and reads the comparison with a thief not in its evil sense of stealing and killing but purely for suddenness and surprise. Wesley admires the technique, calling the abruptness beautiful, and Robertson notes that this is one of the seven beatitudes scattered through the book. Ellicott draws out a second point from the figure: it reminds us not only that the Lord may come unexpectedly, but that he may come and we be unaware of it, since besides the one day when every eye shall see him he comes in various ways to bless and to test men. Vigilance alone, he adds, is not enough — the garments must be kept, since sloth and pleasure will counsel the watcher to lay them aside and rest, while the powers of evil are abroad.

What the garments mean is answered two ways. Barnes takes the picture straightforwardly, of a man who lays his clothes aside and lies down to sleep regardless of danger, so that the thief carries them off and leaves him naked; the essential idea is vigilance, being awake to duty and to danger and not found asleep at one's post. Clarke supplies a precise custom that fits the image exactly. The officer called the overseer of the mountain of the temple went his rounds during the night watches, and any Levite found asleep on guard he had authority to beat with a stick and to burn his vestments; the man then walked home naked, and everyone who saw him knew at once that he had slept at his post and been punished — so that, in the words of the verse, his shame was seen. Robertson notes that the word for shame is a euphemism used elsewhere in the book, and Wesley reads the loss morally, of a man who forfeits the graces he took no care to keep, so that others see both his sin and his punishment.
16:
The verse opens on a grammatical puzzle the commentators refuse to paper over: who is the "he" that gathered them? Gill judges the sense to be rather "they gathered them together", as the Syriac renders it, for though the verb is singular a plural noun stands before it: the unclean spirits just sent out to the kings of the earth are the ones who bring them in. Barnes lays the alternatives side by side. Stuart and De Wette read the neuter plural of the spirits with a singular verb, and Barnes grants their authority enough to show the construction is good Greek, "as indeed no one can doubt"; Hengstenberg makes God the gatherer; others name the sixth angel, or Satan, or the beast, or Christ, and Barnes sends the reader to Poole's Synopsis for the tally. He decides on internal grounds rather than grammatical ones: since the spirits were just described as going out into the whole world precisely to gather the nations to the battle, it is natural they should be the subject here. Robertson agrees on the philology, parsing the second aorist active as singular with the three unclean spirits for its subject, matching the singular verb used of them in the preceding verse.

On the name itself the corpus offers an etymological menu rather than a decision. Clarke sets out three derivations: har-megiddon, "the mount of the assembly"; chormah gedehon, "the destruction of their army"; and har-megiddo, "Mount Megiddo", whose valley he notes was remarkable for two great slaughters, one of the Israelites and one of the Canaanites. He adds that some identify the mount with Carmel as the place of muster. Wesley takes the plainer road: Armageddon signifies the city or the mountain of Megiddo, to which the valley adjoined, a place well known in antiquity for memorable occurrences and in particular for the slaughter of the kings of Canaan related in the book of Judges. Robertson is the most guarded, allowing "the mountains of Megiddo" as perhaps the sense "though not certain", and locating Megiddo in the valley of Esdraelon, where by the waters of the Kishon Israel gained its decisive victory over Sisera. Ellicott supplies the topography the others assume: the high table-land surrounded by hills that was the great battle-field of the Holy Land, where the fortunes of dynasties were decided, where Gideon and Barak triumphed, where Ahaziah and Josiah were slain.

On what the passage means, Ellicott and Clarke converge from opposite tempers. Ellicott lifts the name off the map: "The old battle-ground becomes the symbol of the decisive struggle. It is raised in meaning: it is a type, not a locality." The war of principles, of morals, even of fashion, culminates in an Armageddon, and the struggle in individual men leads the same way to a mountain of decision where the long-wavering heart must take sides and the set of the character be determined — "There is no waving of banners and no prancing of horses' hoofs." Clarke reaches a kindred restraint by way of scorn for those who read the vision off the newspaper: "How ridiculous have been the conjectures of men relative to this point! Within the last twenty years this battle has been fought at various places, according to our purblind seers and self-inspired prophets! At one time it was Austerlitz, at another Moscow, at another Leipsic, and now Waterloo! And thus they have gone on, and will go on, confounding and being confounded." Wesley notes only that the narrative breaks off here, to be resumed much later in the book; Robertson observes that the seer proceeds after the interruption of the preceding beatitude.
17:
The seventh vial is poured out on the air, and the corpus divides over whether that word names a symbol or a medium. Gill and Henry read it as the kingdom of Satan, since he is prince of the power of the air — not that he raises winds at pleasure, Gill is careful to say, but because he commands that host of devils whose dwelling is the air, which encompassing the whole earth stands for his dominion everywhere. Henry draws the consequence: his powers restrained, his policies confounded, he is bound in God's chain; having used every influence to preserve the antichristian interest, blinding judgments and hardening hearts, he can support his tottering cause no longer. Barnes concedes the text does not say why the air, and proposes a physical image: as storms seem engendered there, so this destruction comes as if the whole atmosphere were filled with wind and a desolating whirlwind roused by some invisible power. Clarke reads it as a sign the plague was widely diffused, perhaps portending pestilence, while allowing that the word "may have some emblematical meaning". Robertson makes the simplest case for its severity: all men breathe the air, so this is worse than the smiting of the earth, the sea, the fresh waters, and the sun before it.

On the voice that follows there is no dispute, and the agreement is grammatical as much as theological. Barnes insists it is the voice of God and not of an angel, resting the point on its coming from the throne as well as out of the temple. Ellicott hears in it something like relief, God's own voice proclaiming as though rejoicing in the near approach of the happy end, the last of the last plagues having now gone forth. Robertson supplies the form: a perfect active of the verb of becoming, matching a plural used later in the book, meaning the whole series of plagues is complete. Wesley reads it as the discharge of the order given at the chapter's opening: what was commanded is done. Clarke alone gives the moment a voice of his own, tying it to the promise that in the days of the seventh trumpet the mystery of God should be finished, and then breaking into Latin: "All's over! Fuimus Troes! Ilium fuit! Once there were Trojans, and they had a city; but now all are extinct." Wesley adds only that this is the weightiest vial of all, and seems to take up more time than any before it.

The earthquake that follows produces the chapter's sharpest disagreement about genre. Wesley takes it flatly: one such as had not been since men were upon the earth "was therefore a literal, not figurative, earthquake." Clarke reads the same words as most terrible commotions, both civil and religious, a convulsion or revolution. Ellicott makes it the shaking down of the kingdom of evil itself, completing an overthrow the earlier judgments had only heralded: the throne of the wild beast has been visited, the centre of his power smitten, and now the metropolis of his empire falls. He makes the threefold division a loss of cohesion rather than a partition: the three evil spirits tried to unite all powers in one grand assault, but "there is no natural cohesion among those whose only bond is hatred of good", so the first convulsion shakes them to pieces. The city's identity divides the corpus outright. Gill weighs and rejects Christendom, Jerusalem, and Rome itself before settling on the whole Romish jurisdiction; Barnes and Robertson take it for Babylon, that is Rome; Clarke lists the opinions without choosing; Wesley says plainly it is Jerusalem, set over against Rome and the heathen cities. Robertson catches the note the others leave implicit: Babylon "had not been overlooked. God was simply biding his time with Rome."
20:
Every island flees and the mountains are not found, and the corpus reaches for four different registers to say what that means. Barnes keeps it figurative: language expressive of terrible judgments, as if the very earth were convulsed and everything moved out of its place, the image the sixth seal had used. Clarke goes concrete and political, taking it probably to mean the capture of seaport towns and fortified places. Robertson stays with the physics: islands do sometimes sink in the sea during earthquakes. Gill reaches toward the dissolution of the world itself, the present heavens and earth passing when there will be no more sea and so no islands either. Ellicott declines the topography and reads the scope of the convulsion as the point — so widespread are its effects that every spot is tested, and "there is only one kingdom which cannot be shaken." Wesley registers the sheer physical enormity and then, characteristically, refuses to let it end the story: the islands and mountains were once merely moved out of their place, but here they all flee away. "What a change must this make in the face of the terraqueous globe! And yet the end of the world is not come."

The hail sends nearly everyone to the same two precedents and then to a metrological quarrel. Barnes hears the plague of Egypt; Ellicott hears it too, but adds the defeat of Israel's enemies at Beth-horon, when the Lord cast down great stones from heaven, and says such an overthrow awaits every confederacy arrayed against the kingdom of the righteous King. Gill takes the Beth-horon route first, the kings of the Amorites killed by hail as they fled before Joshua, more slain by the stones than by the sword. Robertson lists both and adds Isaiah and Ezekiel, hail being the settled symbol of God's wrath. On the weight the corpus cannot agree: Barnes gives the Attic talent at about fifty-five pounds Troy and the Jewish at about a hundred and thirteen, and says the horror is easy to conceive on either figure; Robertson reports a range of a hundred and eight to a hundred and thirty pounds in the Greek Old Testament; Wesley simply has each stone at sixty pounds, and draws the trap — from the earthquake men would fly into the fields, but the hail meets them there, and they are no safer if they return indoors. Clarke alone doubts the arithmetic matters, holding the phrase a Greek idiom for something excessively oppressive, and turns aside to ask: "Has this any reference to cannon balls and bombs? It is very doubtful; we are all in the dark in these matters."

What the plague fails to produce is the note on which the corpus ends the chapter. Barnes observes only that men blasphemed God because of the hail, the design of the whole being to show the destruction complete and awful, with the details reserved for later chapters. Robertson makes the point structurally: this punishment had the same effect as the earlier vials that scorched and darkened, and the emphatic positions of the words at the ends of the clause drive it home. Ellicott presses hardest. The discomfiture and the plague work no repentance; the proud, hard spirit that still hates the good remains, "thus is sin its own worst penalty." For an illustration he goes outside the commentators altogether, to Capaneus in Dante's Inferno and the words Virgil addresses to him: "Thou art more punished, in that this thy pride Lives yet unquenched; no torment save thy rage Were to thy fury pain proportioned full." He sets the whole against the one earlier convulsion in the book that ended differently, the earthquake after which the survivors gave glory to the God of heaven. The vials produce terror without repentance, and that, on his reading, is the judgment.
